accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core RF.K.1.d (recognise and name all upper- and lowercase letters), the English national curriculum Year 1 spelling appendix (name the letters of the alphabet in order; use letter names to distinguish between alternative spellings of the same sound) and the DfE Letters and Sounds guidance on letter names versus phonemes. Letter names (aitch, double-u, cue, kay) and every alphabet-train gap and neighbour were rechecked by hand; cat, kid and dog spellings are standard.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-literacy slips: b/d/p/q reversals from mirror generalisation (the flip step and its 'Still b' prediction), 'elemeno' heard as one letter in the song (train step prediction and the LMNOP car), capital and lowercase seen as different letters where shapes differ (A/a, G/g, R/r round), and giving the letter sound when asked for the name (name step options 'kuh: its sound', 'huh: its sound').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagabc is built on the alphabet as a named, ordered set of 26 letters with two cases: partner matching of case pairs, orientation discrimination of b/d/p/q, an ordered alphabet train, name-versus-sound choice and spelling by letter names to choose c or k. flagcaps teaches forming capital strokes, flagprint concepts about print and flagjoin handwriting joins; none of them covers letter naming or alphabet order. The shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child only completes a partner round when every small letter is on the capital with the same name, finds by tapping that d is not accepted when b is asked, places N into the l-m-?-o-p train and sees five separate cars, and spells cat only when choosing see over kay, so the case, orientation, order and naming ideas are found by doing before the done text names them.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'No, two letters' for G and g, 'Still b' for a mirrored b, and 'Yes, one letter' for elemeno. Each task straight after makes the child act against the wrong option (g goes on G, the flipped shape is a different tile, the train needs N between M and O) and the done message quotes the guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers: chose n for R, chose the capital itself, L before M, skipped N to O, gave the sss sound for the name of s, gave see (the name of c), said a flipped b is still b, chose p, chose k for cat, said either spelling is fine. Every tag has its own correction naming the slip; the lab steps also give per-tap messages such as 'b and d are flipped'.

readability.evidence: Kid text is short sentences for a family read-aloud ('Turn b around and it is d!') scores FK -0.2 against the family kid limit of 5.0; adult text scores FK 8.6 against 10 while using the exact terms alphabet knowledge, letter name, letter sound or phoneme, upper- and lowercase, capital, alphabetical order, reversal and mirror generalisation, and the standard codes RF.K.1.d and Year 1 spelling.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph shows one concrete letter fact with an example; the adult paragraphs carry the curriculum statements, the name/sound distinction, four named mistakes and the lab outline. Explanation overlap with the capital letters, print and syllables lessons stays under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 light and iPhone 13 dark show three letter tiles at least 60 px wide over three capital boxes, the five-car train readable with the gap outlined in violet, four b/d/p/q tiles across the width, the cat picture with three spelling slots, and big young-mode buttons below the canvas. phone_sweep reported 0 findings on iPhone and Android.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone, no console errors, every Show me completed. Every drag has a button twin (Pick a letter, On S/M/T, and one button per tile with labels such as 'The name is aitch'), and the canvas aria-label speaks each change, e.g. 'Picked small g. Now pick its capital.'
